newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - U.S.,Japan face off at WTO over photofilm.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S.,Japan face off at WTO over photofilm.

text.p: Member countries of the World Trade Organisation on Wednesday agreed to set up a panel to rule on a complaint by the United States that Japan rigs its photofilm market to keep out foreign suppliers.

And in a surprise move, the European Union said it reserved its rights to take part in the case -- indicating that it sympathised with the U.S. view and might provide the panel with supporting argument.

The multi-billion dollar dispute -- behind which stands a struggle between the Eastman Kodak and Fuji photo giants to penetrate each other's domestic markets -- was the first major U.S.-Japan trade row to get so far in the WTO.

Senior envoys from both sides -- U.S. trade ambassador Booth Gardner and Japan's WTO mission chief Nobutoshi Akao -- each told reporters they were convinced the case would end in their country's favour after what could be a year-long process.

"We have a very strong case, and we are sure the panel will see that," said Gardner after the WTO's increasingly busy Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) set the procedure in motion for the convening of the three-man trade tribunal.
"We are sure we can win," said Akao. "There are no serious grounds for the U.S. complaint."

And he told the DSB the U.S. claims were "totally contrary to the facts" and argued that government measures Washington says were shaped to undermine free trade accords signed by Tokyo were not aimed at excluding imports.

EU acting head of mission Ian Wilkinson told reporters Brussels had asked to be associated with the case as a third party "because there is a sizeable (European) Community firm that has a substantial interests in the japanese market."

He declined to specify, but the German Agfa Gevaert company has a small but growing share of the Japanese market but trade sources say it has also complained of the hidden barriers Kodak argues have deprived it of $5,6 billion over the last decade.
Agfa is the photofilm and products unit of the chemicals giant Bayer AG.

The U.S. company, which provides some 10 per cent of the photofilm and paper sold in Japan, welcomed the establishment of the panel, expected to start hearings within the next month and due to deliver its verdict next spring.
The decision can be challenged by either side and would then go to an appeals panel.

"Today's action signifies the beginning of the WTO's formal investigation into anti-competitive trade practices supported by the government of Japan," said a statement from Kodak, based in Rochester, New York.

Kodak and Fuji between them dominate global sales of photofilm, with the U.S. firm holding 36 per cent and the Japanese giant 33 per cent. Agfa is third, but far behind the big two on the world scene.

However, in the United States Fuji -- which has recently made fresh inroads by winning control of a major film processing network -- holds only around 12 per cent of the market to Kodak's 70 per cent, a mirror image of the situation in Japan.

Japanese officials and Fuji lawyers argue that Kodak has failed to move fast enough to introduce new products in Japan. They also say that market share can be explained by a consumer preference in both countries for the national brand.

Spokesman Keith Rockwell said the WTO, which replaced the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) 22 months ago, saw the fact the case had been brought to the DSB as a sign of the confidence in the body of the 124 member states.
